title: Run two threads by hand
starter:
let run (schedule : int list) : int =
  let counter = ref 0 in
  let reg = [| 0; 0 |] in
  let step = [| 0; 0 |] in
  List.iter (fun t ->
    (match step.(t) mod 3 with
     | 0 -> reg.(t) <- !counter
     | 1 -> ()
     | _ -> ());
    step.(t) <- step.(t) + 1) schedule;
  !counter
hints: Each thread does three steps in turn: load, add, store. The load is written. Which two branches still do nothing?
The add step changes only the thread's own register: `reg.(t) <- reg.(t) + 1`. It must not read `counter` again.
The store step copies the register back: `counter := reg.(t)`. With the schedule `[0; 1; 0; 1; 0; 1]` both threads load 0, so both store 1.

answer.code:
let run (schedule : int list) : int =
  let counter = ref 0 in
  let reg = [| 0; 0 |] in
  let step = [| 0; 0 |] in
  List.iter (fun t ->
    (match step.(t) mod 3 with
     | 0 -> reg.(t) <- !counter
     | 1 -> reg.(t) <- reg.(t) + 1
     | _ -> counter := reg.(t));
    step.(t) <- step.(t) + 1) schedule;
  !counter
answer.explain: Adding 1 to shared memory is three steps: load it into a register, add, store it back. When one thread runs all three before the other starts, both additions count. When the steps interleave, both threads load the same old value and one addition is lost. The code is correct line by line. Only the order of steps differs, and that is what makes a race hard to find by testing.
